Gurupūrṇimā
(Āṣāḍha Pūrṇimā)
------------------------------------------
Kṛṣṇa द्वैपायन, better known as व्यास-महर्षि, did yeoman service to the cause of Vedic studies by gathering all the Vedic hymns extant during his times, dividing them into four parts based on their use in the sacrificial rites and teaching them to his four chief disciples पैल, वैशम्पायन, जैमिनि and सुमन्तु. It was this dividing and editing of the वेदस् that earned him the honorific ‘Vyāsa’ (vyas = to divide, to edit). Since he thus occupies the place of a great गुरु or preceptor, his birthday—Āṣāḍha-pūrṇimā, full-मोओन् day in the month of आषाढ, generally in July—is known as ‘Vyāsapūrṇimā’ or ‘Gurupūrṇimā’. The day is considered as sacred, not only to the saṁnyāsins (ascetics) but also to the students of Vedic studies.
Since the गुरु or आचार्य or the preceptor occupies a very exalted place in Hindu religious traditions, गुरुपूर्णिमा is sacred to one and all. On this day people are expected to worship or honour their gurus or teachers, especially the spiritual preceptors.
In the olden days, saṁnyāsins used to lead an itinerant life. Since this was not possible in the four months of the rainy season (Āṣāḍha to Kārttika, corresponding to July-October), they were permitted to stay at one place during this period. This was technically called ‘Cāturmāsya,’ meaning ‘the religious rite to be observed during the period of the four months’.
The Cāturmāsyavrata started on the गुरुपूर्णिमा day with the worship of व्यास, one’s own गुरु and beginning of scriptural studies including their exposition to those that seek knowledge. The laity were expected to take advantage of this opportunity to serve the saṁyāsins and get instructions from them about religion and spiritual values.
In the Vedic period, there were sacrifices known as Cāturmāsyas. They were the three sacrifices वैश्वदेव, वरुणप्रघास and साकमेध performed at four-monthly intervals. This चातुर्मास्य started with the performance of the वरुणप्रघास on the आषाढ-pūrṇimā day, the other two being done on Kārttikapūrṇimā (Sākamedha) and चैत्र-Pūrṇimā (Vaiśvadeva) days. The yajamāna or performer (of these sacrifices) was ordained to observe certain disciplines during this period, such as sleeping on the ground, avoiding luxurious ड़ोओद् and bodily decorations, observing continence and so on.
When, over the centuries, there was a gradual metamorphosis of the Vedic sacrificial rites into temple rites and pūjās or worship of the deity at home, the Vedic चातुर्मास्य might have quietly assumed the form of the Cāturmāsyavrata of the पुराणस्, which is prevalent even now. This vrata which is open to all, commences from the गुरुपूर्णिमा day. It is spread over the period of four months up to Kārttīkapūrṇimā. During this period, the performer had to abjure many comforts and good things of life like sleeping on a cot, consuming tasty foods (especially honey, milk, curds and vegetables) and so on. The vrata was to be concluded by worshipping God, feeding the ब्राह्मणस् and giving them gifts according to one’s capacity. This Cāturmāsyavrata was declared to be capable of conferring many favours pertaining to this life like good ड़ोओद्, beauty, intelligence, progeny and so on.

Guruvāyūr
(‘town established by गुरु [Bṛhaspati] and वायु’)
------------------------------------------
Introduction
One of the well-known and popular places of पिल्ग्रिमगे, especially for the devotees of कृष्ण, is गुरुवायूर् in the Kerala State. It is a small town situated to the west of the city of Triśśūr or Trichur, at a distance of 30 kms. (20 miles). It is famous for its temple of श्रीकृष्ण, the deity being fondly called Guruvāyūrappan (father or master of गुरुवायूर्).
Local Legends
According to the स्थलपुराण or the local legends based on the Nāradīyapurāṇa (Gurupavanapuramāhātmya), the image was being worshipped at द्वारका by श्रीकृष्ण himself. When the city was submerged, he gave it to his disciple उद्धव with the instruction that, in consultation with गुरु (Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of gods) and वायु (the wind-god), it should be installed in a suitable holy place. When गुरु and वायु came to the south, in search of a suitable place, the great sage परशुराम helped them to find one and got it installed in a beautiful temple.
Thus, according to this traditional account, the temple is at least 5000 years old.
कृष्ण Temple at गुरुवायूर्">Śrī कृष्ण Temple at GuruvāyūrKing जनमेजय, the great grandson of the Pāṇḍava hero अर्जुन, is said to have worshipped this deity to get rid of his leprosy which he had contracted by the performance of the सर्पयाग (serpent-sacrifice) to exterminate the entire race of serpents. (See JANAMEJAYA for details.)
A Brief History
Historically speaking, the earliest references to this temple are available only from the 16th century onwards.
During the various political turmoils that South India had to face, the temple suffered many times at the hands of the Dutch (A. D. 1756), Haidar Alī (A. D. 1766) and Ṭippu Sultān (A. D. 1789). It was ultimately saved by the princes of the Zamorin family in A. D. 1792.
From A. D. 1825 onwards, the condition of the temple improved, mainly due to the dedicated services of the Ulanāḍ Paṇikkars’ family.
The eastern gopuram (tower) was rebuilt in A. D. 1842. Renovations and beautifications of the central shrine and the मण्डप (open auditorium) as also of the ध्वजस्तम्भ (flag-staff), were carried out in A. D. 1892. Several administrative reforms were introduced from A. D. 1900 onwards. Temple doors were thrown open to the people of the lower castes, hitherto treated as untouchables, from A. D. 1931. Gold-casing of the ध्वजस्तम्भ was completed in A. D. 1952.
In A. D. 1970, a disastrous fire destroyed a major part of the buildings, the main shrine and the subsidiary ones being miraculously untouched. Very soon, the temple-complex was restored to its original form.
The Presiding Deity
The main deity in the sanctum sanctorum—called Śrīkoil—is that of नारायण in the standing posture. It is made of a rare stone called पाताल-añjanam (black bismuth). It has four arms carrying the शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). It is adorned with a तुलसी (holy basil) garland and a pearl necklace. The walls of the Śrīkoil are adorned with paintings depicting boy कृष्ण’s pastimes.
The Temple Complex
The main temple is rather small in size and has been built in the typical Kerala style of architecture, with a wooden roof covered with copper plates, over the main shrine. It faces east and is usually entered from that direction.
गुरुवायूर् Temple">Deity at गुरुवायूर् TempleThe eastern gateway, called Bhūvai-kuṇṭham, is the main entrance. The ध्वजस्तम्भ is gold-plated and is 33.5 metres (110 ft.) high. On either side of it, there are two dīpastambhas (pillars of lamps), 7 metres (22 ft.) in height with 13 circular receptacles for lighting the lamps.
Surrounding the गर्भगृह or the sanctum, is a pillared hall known as Nālambalam. On the outside of the northern wall surrounding the sanctum is the viḷakkumatam, a gallery of 11 rows of 6614 tiny lamps that are lit on festival days.
On the outside of the whole structure, there is a paved path for processions called mātilakam.
Other structures in this area are: the stage for कृष्ण-aṭṭam (dance drama on कृष्ण); two vātilmatams (raised platforms with carved pillars); temple kitchen; shrines for गणेश and शास्ता (or अय्यप्पन्).
It is interesting to note that there is a permanently closed cell on the western side of the kitchen, believed to होउसे many precious jewels and guarded by the Pañcanāgas (five divine serpents).
Other temples at and near गुरुवायूर् are: शिव-पार्वती temple at Mammiyūr to the north-west; नारायणी temple to the north of Mammiyūr; Pārthasārathi temple, believed to be more than 1000 years old; Tiruveṅkaṭam temple near the above one; Perutaṭṭa शिव temple to the south of गुरुवायूर् temple, at a distance of one kilometre.
Rites and Rituals
The main temple at गुरुवायूर् follows an elaborate system of rites and rituals initiated by शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820). There are five main pūjas (worship) per day spread over the period 3 A.M. to 10 P.M. The उत्सवमूर्ति (processional image) is taken round the main shrine twice a day, mounted on an elephant.
The darśan (seeing the deity) at 3 A.M. with all the flowers and garlands of the previous day, is considered extremely auspicious. This is known as nirmālya-दर्शन (nirmālya = used flowers, to be removed and thrown away in a place set apart for it). Usually there will be a heavy crowd of devotees for this.
One of the popular modes of offering by the devotees is the tulābhāram. It is the ritual of weighing oneself against a specified material like bananas, sugar, jaggery, coconuts, sandalwood and so on. The material is then gifted to the temple.
Festivals
The following are the most important of the numerous festivals conducted in this temple:
Gītājayantī; Viṣu (New year’s day which falls generally on the 15th April); Akṣayyatṛtīyā (in April/May); Brahmotsavam or Utsavam, the main annual festival spread over ten days, during February/March, an elephant race being a great attraction.
The last day of the Utsavam is observed as the special bathing festival of the Lord at the temple-tank called Rudratīrtha.
Next to this tank is the temple of भगवती (Divine मोथेर्). At this temple, the नवरात्र festival is observed on a grand scale.
The other festivals are Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī (in August/September) and कुचेल’s Day (first Wednesday in Mārgaśira (December/January).
Cultural Programmes
Several cultural programmes and religious discourses are conducted under the aegis of the गुरुवायूर् temple. They are: Kṛṣṇāṭṭam; Kūṭṭu; भागवत Saptāha; recital of the Nārāyaṇīyam.
The Kṛṣṇāṭṭam is a dance-drama with characters acting their roles while the story is narrated by others. So also the singing. It is enacted on nine days, with one theme from कृष्ण’s life (except the last scene of कृष्ण’s ascension) on each day, between 10 P.M. and 3 A.M. A special permanent stage has been erected in the north-western part of the processional path (mātilakam).
The Kūṭṭu is a mono-acting performance by a talented artist, the themes being selected from the two epics as also the Bhāgavata. Humour and wit are the keynotes of this performance. It is enacted at the place reserved for it in the south-east corner, the place being called kūṭṭambaḷam.
The भागवत-saptāha—recital of the Bhāgavata spread over seven days—is conducted quite often.
The Nārāyaṇīyam is an extremely famous and popular work in the Kerala State. It is a condensed version—but an original work—of the Bhāgavata by Meppattūr नारायण Bhaṭṭātiripād (A. D. 1560-1625). (See NĀRĀYAṆA BHAṬṬĀTIRI.) A recital of this work is also conducted regularly in the temple.
God of Miracles
Innumerable miracles have been attributed to the grace of the Lord here by the faithful. The votaries belonging to non-Hindu faiths too are being drawn towards this deity.
The gingelly-oil used in the bathing of the image during अभिषेक (ceremonial bath) is in great demand since it is believed to be a sure medicine for arthritis and similar diseases.
It is interesting to note here, the story of the temple elephant (tusker) Keśavan by name. It served the temple during all the festivals and ceremonies, for 62 years, including the carrying of the tiḍambu (golden howdah) for 54 years. It was extremely docile and friendly. It died quietly and suddenly in A. D. 1976, in front of the chief gateway, as if bowing down to the deity. A life-size image of this elephant had been installed in the campus and its day of demise is celebrated with a procession of decorated elephants.
Finis
While visiting a holy place, a pilgrim expects not only spiritual solace but also the fulfilment of his desires which he is unable to achieve through normal human efforts. The गुरुवायूर् temple has certainly succeeded in fulfilling such hopes and aspirations of its votaries if judged from the numerous experiences of numberless devotees.
There is no wonder then, that year by year, the number of pilgrims is swelling, contributions by them is increasing, thus making it one of the few most popular temples of India with a fabulous income which is being properly utilised by the temple management.

Gurudvāra
(‘gateway to the गुरु’)
------------------------------------------
All religious communities have their own places of worship and prayer, be it a temple or a church or a mosque. The place of worship of the Sikhs is the गुरुद्वार (also spelt as ‘gurdvāra’).
Gurudvāra-Place of worship of the SikhsGuru Gobind Singh (A. D. 1666-1708) the tenth and the last गुरु, ordained that there would be no more human Gurus and that the Book, the Ādi Granth (compiled by the fifth गुरु, Arjan) itself should be looked upon as the गुरु after him.
A गुरुद्वार is the place where this book, the Ādi Granth—also called Guru Granth Sāhib—is kept in a hall with all the paraphernalia needed to honour it like a human गुरु.
The Book, once established, is looked after, by the granthis (scripture-readers). It is also taken out in a procession like the उत्सव-vigraha, (processional deity) in a Hindu temple.
The गोल्देन् तेम्प्ले (called Hari Mandir or Darbār Sāhib) at Amritsar in Punjab is the chief गुरुद्वार of the Sikhs. The other important ones are at Kapurthala, Anandpur (both in Punjab), Nanded (Maharashtra) and Patna (Bihar).

Gurmukhi script
------------------------------------------
The survival of a religion depends very much upon its basic scripture. The survival of this scripture, again, depends on its being committed to writing.
When सिखिस्म् came into existence and started becoming popular, especially with the masses, it became necessary to compile the sayings of its founder गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539). गुरु Aṅgad (A. D. 1504-1552) took the trouble of getting the scripture committed to writing. He modified the Laṇḍā script, then in existence, by borrowing letters from other scripts like the Śāradā, the Ṭhākurī and the Nāgarī. The present script has 35 letters. It is called the Punjabi script. Since it was done by the Sikh गुरु Aṅgad, it was also called the गुर्मुखि स्च्रिप्त्. The fifth गुरु, Arjan Dev (A. D. 1563-1607), compiled the Ādi Granth in this script.
The गुर्मुखि स्च्रिप्त् has 3 vowels and 32 consonants. There are no conjunct consonants. Words like ‘Bhagavān’ are written as ‘Pahagvān’.

gurudakṣiṇā
(‘honorarium [paid to the] गुरु’)
------------------------------------------
Education was considered in ancient and medieval India as too sacred an act to demand or accept any fee. If, however, a disciple wanted to give something to his गुरु, at the time of his departure from the गुरुकुल, as a mark of his gratitude, the गुरु could accept it. This could take two forms: accepting whatever the disciple gave, or, asking for something which one really wanted.
Though offering of money, cows or land was common, uncommon or even odd or novel things were sometimes asked for as गुरुदक्षिणा. द्रोणाचार्य wanted the Pāṇḍavas to capture the king Drupada and bring to him! उदङ्क, a sage, had to take a lot of trouble to bring and give the ear-rings of the queen Madavatī to अहल्या, the wife of his गुरु, गौतम.
However, the idea has always been there that the debt to one’s गुरु can never be repaid.

gurukula
(‘house of the गुरु’)
------------------------------------------
In ancient and medieval India edu-cation was generally residential. The students had to reside in the houses of their gurus. This gave them not only greater opportunities to learn the sciences and the arts, with all their intricacies and secrets, but also get inspiration for their life from that of their gurus.
When the number of students that the teachers kept in their houses grew quite large, these houses grew into institutions called ‘gurukulas’. And, they were maintained by the society, especially the kings and the rich persons, who endowed these gurukulas with sufficient property and funds, so that they could provide quality एदुचतिओन्, free of cost, to all the students.
In these gurukulas, attention was paid not only for the physical welfare and intellectual development but also for spiritual growth so that the students could develop a wholesome personality.
It was not uncommon to find as many as ten thousand students in some of the bigger institutions. Not only out of necessity but also as a good practice, the senior and better-qualified students were made to teach the novices and also supervise over their life and discipline.
Though punishments for transgressions existed, they were not very severe. Incorrigible students were expelled to save the discipline and reputation of the institution.

guruvṛtti
(‘behaviour before the गुरु’)
------------------------------------------
In the ancient days, एदुचतिओन् was imparted in the gurukulas or the houses of the gurus, the preceptors. A ब्रह्मचारिन् (the Vedic student) was expected to follow strictly a code of conduct prescribed for him. That part of it, which concerned his behaviour (= वृत्ति) before the गुरु, was called ‘guruvṛtti’.
The Vedic student was expected to desire the welfare of his गुरु always. He was to be diligent in his studies even if he was not specifically directed to do so. He was to cultivate a very pure and reverential attitude towards the गुरु. He was also to avoid any type of ostentation before him. He should never sit in his presence, unless permitted to do so. He should never speak ill of or criticise his गुरु before anyone at anytime nor listen to such words if others are doing so. He must never address his गुरु by his name (vide Manusmṛti, Second Chapter).

guru
(‘one who is praised [due to his great qualities]’ ‘one who teaches [the śāstras like the वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
In Hindu religion and culture, every science or art or craft has to be learnt directly from a competent teacher in that field. Since learning is considered as a तपस् (austerity, discipline), the teacher has to be looked upon with great respect and reverence.
A teacher of the scriptures is called an adhyāpaka or an उपाध्याय or an आचार्य. The former two teach the chanting of the वेदस् whereas the last one teaches their meaning and significance also.
The word ‘guru’ is used in a more comprehensive sense. It has sometimes been defined as one who dispels the dark-ness of इग्नोरन्चे. It invariably refers to a spiritual teacher, an advanced सोउल्, who is an expert not only in the knowledge of the scriptures but also well-established in ब्रह्मन् or God (vide Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
A गुरु should be a person of pure parentage, of a sinless life and great self-control. Apart from having a deep knowledge of the scriptures, he should be an adept in the various modes of meditation and worship also. He must be the very personification of compassion and love towards his disciples.
A disciple is expected to look upon his गुरु as if he is God himself. However, the Hindu scriptures also warn the people against false gurus.
Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods in हेअवेन् is also known as गुरु.
Guru is also the name of the planet जुपितेर्. (See BṚHASPATI.)
‘Guru’ was also the nickname of प्रभाकर (A. D. 700?), a prominent teacher of the पूर्वमीमाṁसा school of philosophy.
The word ‘guru’ has been used widely in the Sanskrit works in several other senses such as: ड़थेर्, मोथेर्, husband, any teacher in any field of knowledge and God himself.
See also ĀCĀRYA.
